"Relax, Didi. I'm a night person. The panic is my fuel." Sharmila cracked her knuckles over the laptop.
"You said that about the lab file too."
"And I got it done!"

"Coincidence." She grinned. "Honestly, I feel so awake right now. The words just come."

"It's fine," Sharmila whispered. "It's done."
"Is it the way you wanted?"
A long silence. "No."

Mentor's note, Ishita, architecture studio, 14 March
Aditi arrived at 9:40, forty minutes past the jury deadline, model still wet with glue and one wall missing. Third time this term. Aditi told me cheerfully, "I'm a pressure person; my best ideas come at 3 a.m." The concept really was strong. But the joints were sloppy, the drawings unlabelled, and Aditi's hands were shaking, perhaps from no sleep and too much tea. When I asked when the work began, the answer was "last night, properly".
What I did: I didn't lecture. I asked Aditi to try one experiment on the next project: a rough cardboard model due to me a week early. I said the 3 a.m. energy can go into refining, not building. We meet again on Friday, and I'll ask how the early version felt.

The college in Hoshangabad had one printer, and it closed at 10 a.m. Mridul's project report was due at 10:30.
At 9 p.m. the night before, he hadn't started. He grinned at his friend Neelam across the hostel verandah. “Watch me. Pressure is when I shine.”
And for a while he did. His fingers flew. He felt alive, buzzing, almost happy.
By 2 a.m. the power went off. He wrote by candle. By 5, his head was pounding.
At 9:45 he ran to the printer with a pen drive. The report had two pages in the wrong order and no references.
Neelam, who had finished hers last week, handed him a glass of water. “Did you shine?”
Mridul, pale and sweating, managed a laugh. “For about three hours.”

Rafael had always said he wrote best at 3 a.m. At his university in Lisbon, it was a bit of a legend. His flatmate Jin had seen it many times: nothing for two weeks, then a wild all-nighter, loud music, energy drinks, and a paper finished at dawn.
This semester Rafael had three papers due in the same week. He left all three.
The first all-nighter went fine. He felt thrilled, like a hero in a film. The second, his hands shook. The third, he fell asleep at the desk at 4 a.m. and woke at 8, with half a page done.
Jin found him staring at his screen, grey-faced. “You okay?”
“I don't think the panic works when there are three,” Rafael said.
He got an extension on the third paper, but lost marks. He also caught a cold that lasted two weeks.
